idea.text: Some ions from two clear solutions can join to make a solid that won't dissolve. The solid suddenly appears as a cloudy precipitate, and its colour helps identify which ions were there.
idea.analogy: Like a crowded dance floor: most people keep moving around, but certain pairs grab each other and sit down together, and those pairs are the solid that drops out.

steps.title: Put on goggles
steps.instruction: Barium salts are toxic and NaOH is corrosive. Goggles on.

steps.title: Copper sulfate into tube 1
steps.instruction: Pour about 2 mL of copper(II) sulfate into tube 1.

whatIf.order: Without goggles, one splash in the eye can cause serious, sometimes permanent, damage within seconds. That's why goggles go on before you open any bottle.
whatIf.rate: A fast pour into a narrow test tube splashes the solution out.
whatIf.overshoot: More copper sulfate means you'll need more drops of sodium hydroxide before you see a lot of precipitate.
whatIf.quantity: The amount changes how much precipitate you can make, not what colour it is.

explore.then: You'd need more drops of sodium hydroxide before all the copper ions are used up, and you'd get more blue precipitate.

steps.title: NaOH dropwise
steps.instruction: Add sodium hydroxide drop by drop. Watch where each drop lands.

whatIf.order: Copper sulfate goes in first so the drops have copper ions to react with.
whatIf.not-dropwise: Pouring sodium hydroxide in fast hides where the precipitate forms and wastes a corrosive chemical. Drop by drop, you see the blue solid appear where each drop lands.

explore.if: add a lot of extra sodium hydroxide
explore.then: More blue precipitate forms until all the copper ions are used up. Copper hydroxide doesn't redissolve in dilute sodium hydroxide.

explore.if: use iron(II) sulfate instead of copper sulfate
explore.then: You'd get a green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide. A different metal ion gives a different coloured precipitate, which is how chemists identify them.

steps.title: Barium chloride into tube 2
steps.instruction: Pour about 2 mL of barium chloride into tube 2.

whatIf.order: Without goggles, one splash in the eye can cause serious, sometimes permanent, damage within seconds. That's why goggles go on before you open any bottle.
whatIf.rate: A fast pour splashes toxic barium chloride solution. Pour gently.
whatIf.overshoot: More barium chloride means more precipitate once the sulfate goes in, and more toxic waste to dispose of.
whatIf.quantity: The amount changes how much precipitate forms, not its colour.

steps.title: Sodium sulfate dropwise
steps.instruction: Add sodium sulfate drop by drop.

whatIf.order: Barium chloride goes in first so the drops have barium ions to react with.
whatIf.not-dropwise: Pouring the sulfate in fast means you miss the moment the white solid first appears. Drop by drop shows it forming.

explore.then: Chemists add acid first in the sulfate test so carbonate ions can't give a false white precipitate. Barium sulfate still forms.

explore.if: use sodium chloride instead of sodium sulfate
explore.then: No precipitate: barium chloride dissolves, so Ba²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions just stay in solution.

safe-1.text: What protects your eyes from splashes?

safe-2.text: Drag the goggles onto your face icon before handling the reagents.

vol-1.text: You only need a small volume: about a fifth of the tube.

vol-2.text: Tilt just past the pour point and stop at 2 mL on the counter.

drop-1.text: Add slowly so you can see where the solid first forms.

drop-2.text: Tap the dropper bottle one drop at a time.

observations.whatHappened: Clear blue copper sulfate gave a pale blue cloudy solid as soon as NaOH landed. Barium chloride and sodium sulfate, both colourless, made a thick white solid. Both solids slowly settled to the bottom.
observations.why: Some pairs of ions form compounds that hardly dissolve. When their concentrations multiplied together exceed the solubility product (Ksp), the extra comes out of solution as a solid precipitate.
realWorld: Barium meals for X-rays (BaSO₄ is insoluble, so safe)

prompts.question: The pale blue precipitate in tube 1 is...
prompts.explain: Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂, a pale blue solid.

prompts.question: Which ions made the white solid in tube 2?
prompts.explain: Barium sulfate is the insoluble one; NaCl stays dissolved.

captions.text: Goggles on: barium salts are toxic.
captions.why: Precipitation tests identify ions in solution, but some of the chemicals used are hazardous.
captions.safety: Barium compounds are toxic if swallowed and sodium hydroxide is corrosive. Goggles on, small volumes, and no hand-to-mouth.

captions.text: Copper sulfate, then sodium hydroxide drop by drop...
captions.why: Cu²⁺ ions meet OH⁻ ions and form copper(II) hydroxide, a pale blue solid that doesn't dissolve in water.

captions.text: Barium chloride meets sodium sulfate: a thick white precipitate.
captions.why: Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ form barium sulfate, which hardly dissolves at all, so it appears almost instantly. This is the test for sulfate ions.
